# Your AI Agents Can Multitask. Can You?

YOUR AI AGENTS CAN MULTITASK. CAN YOU? https://every.?ev_audience=free


MANAGING SEVERAL AGENTS MEANS CONSTANT CONTEXT SWITCHING. HERE’S HOW NINE PEOPLE AT EVERY HANDLE IT. https://every.?ev_audience=free

by Arielle Shipper https://every.?ev_audience=free

Today my Dot https://every.?ev_audience=free Sebastian told me, “In one 29-minute stretch this morning, you brought me 7 different lines of work.” I usually find Sebastian helpful, but that observation was terrifying. It was true: In 29 minutes, I had set agents working on everything from a strategic review of company priorities to documentation for a visa application. Is this what productivity in the age of AI looks like?



Until recently, I was Every’s whole operations department. I ran meetings, paid invoices, provisioned logins, articulated company strategy, programmed offsites, stocked our office with snacks, and responded to piles of Slack messages every day by myself. I could do that because I had a team of AI agents working for me.

In a previous life, planning a weeklong companywide onsite would have involved creating a Google Sheet with jobs like planning facilitated sessions and making buddy pairs and then methodically diving into each task. Last month, I opened a single orchestrator thread to plan our Think Week and asked the agent to spin up subthreads for each task. The subagents worked in parallel while I periodically checked in and gave approvals. These days, I can get more work done than I ever thought possible.

I also face a persistent struggle to think deeply about any of it.

In the allocation economy https://every.?ev_audience=free, the bottleneck is not doing the work but directing the work. While waiting for your agents to complete the multiple tasks you’ve assigned them, you might move to another task in the name of staying productive. Suddenly, you’ve worked on 16 things in two hours.

This new way of working can help us ship things faster than ever, but often at the cost of thinking deeply and strategically about what we’re doing. Researchers are starting to measure that cost. In a survey of nearly 1,500 U.S. workers https://every.?ev_audience=free, Boston Consulting Group found that people overseeing multiple AI agents were among the most likely to report “brain fry,” mental fatigue from using or supervising AI beyond their cognitive capacity. That fatigue came with more errors, greater decision fatigue, and a stronger intention to quit.

At Every, we all experience this new way of working differently. I asked colleagues in various roles across the team what systems and frameworks they use to work effectively while constantly context switching. Here’s what I learned.

https://every.?ev_audience=free




YOUR ROADMAP NEEDS MORE THAN A .MD FILE.

Your agent has a plan. Your team still needs to agree on the priorities.

Which customer problem comes first? What evidence backs it up? What changes when you learn something new?

Jira Product Discovery brings customer insights, prioritization, and living roadmaps into one shared place. Connect ideas to delivery in Jira so people and agents understand what to build and why.

Keep using AI to move faster. Give everyone a shared view of where you’re going and why.

MAKE THE WORK VISIBLE

Every’s social lead Becky Isjwara crafts social strategy, creates content, and tracks metrics, and AI is involved in much of it: She drafts with Codex, copyedits with Every Agent https://every.?ev_audience=free, and uses Flora and Hyperframes to generate visual assets.

On a typical day, she might start drafting tweets, only to get distracted by a pileup of Slack notifications, including a request to create a YouTube thumbnail. She kicks off a Codex thread to generate it, checks mentions on X while she waits, and forgets about the task that started it all: drafting tweets. New model releases with more capabilities have only made her “shiny toy syndrome” worse, leading to more jumbled thoughts and half-finished threads. Using AI is “like having superpowers,” Becky says. “I can take on more tasks than before and push them further, but I feel like a Marvel superhero that has no idea how to control them.”

Becky’s solution is to go 50 percent analog, 50 percent AI-native. She keeps a pen and pad by her computer so she can write down every task and agent she has running. She pairs that list with her Dot, which she named Sox, as her control center: an orchestrator that opens subthreads as needed and handles quick tasks without her having to navigate between chats.

Try it: Use analog methods if they help, and have an agent keep the running list for you.

Prompt

You’re my control center for today. Every time I start a task or delegate work to an agent, add it to a running list with [the task, where it’s running, and what I’m waiting on]. When I return from a break or a meeting, show me the running list and ask which item I’d like to tackle next.


DECIDE BEFORE YOUR WORK STARTS

As an engineer on the Every Agent team, Lee Knowlton is always developing several features at once, some of which require multiple threads to build. Through trial and error, he learned that his productivity maxes out at two active projects: a main project and a subproject, while other persistent tasks run in the background. “I previously tried to do five sessions at a time, which became too much context to juggle and was draining,” he says.

Recently, he was building two features for Every Agent, one focused on tool capabilities and one focused on user experience (UX). The tool project could largely be checked with automated tests, so he used his Dot to kick off parallel threads for it. That freed him to stay focused on the UX feature, which required more human judgment, in a single thread. “I think it’s important to understand your mental cost of context switching and what you end up compromising on the end product,” he says. “You can lose valuable and important parts of the work.”

Lee’s other secret is planning. Before a project starts, he maps out the next several hours of work: the end goal, which elements have a metric that AI can optimize for, which can use AI as a judge with human supervision, and which require his subjective taste. He also counterplans, forecasting what might go wrong (including lost focus) and building in guardrails against it.

Kieran Klaassen https://every.?ev_audience=free, a member of the frontier team, is the creator of the Compound Engineering plugin https://every.?ev_audience=free. He has always had more ideas than he could act on, and running work in parallel finally lets him pursue them. The plugin is designed to require human input at the start of his work, because that’s when he’s making the creative decisions. Stronger models have raised the stakes of that early thinking, since he can now set a more ambitious goal and have agents work on it overnight. He likes taking an hour to set up as many as six projects or big bets he has thought through carefully, then leaving them to run. Ideally, every decision is made before execution begins; if the agents need his input after that, he counts it as a failure.

Kieran finds the work addictive and hard not to do, so he has to set limits on purpose. He picks his top three priorities each day as a north star. Some days he decides in advance to keep a single thread open and work on one thing.

Paridhi Agarwal https://every.?ev_audience=free, also an engineer on the Every Agent team, usually keeps three to five Claude Code sessions open. She flips between tabs to see which agent is done, reviews its work, and hands it the next task before circling back. That rhythm suits smaller bugs and one-off tasks. Harder work usually gets her full attention, because splitting it across tabs means “the main task takes much longer.” The exception is hard work with a concrete, step-by-step plan, which she runs across several sessions at once.

What keeps the parallel sessions from colliding is plain, fixed structure. A short skill sets the pipeline every bug fix follows: The agent writes and checks the code, then stops and asks Paridhi to review before anything is merged. “If I make a skill too complex, the agent gets worse at following it, because there are a lot of conflicting instructions in there,” she says. “What I learned is that simple structure beats complex setups.”

The structure keeps the code in order, but it hasn’t settled her attention. “I leave a lot of agents idle, and things keep piling up through the week, and that gets to me a lot,” she says. Closing tabs and finishing one piece of work before checking on another helps most, “and it’s something I need to practice more.”

Try it: Before a multihour block of focused time, sort your work into tasks an agent can verify on its own and tasks that require your judgment.

Prompt

Here’s what I want to get done in the next [number] hours: [list]. For each item, tell me whether AI could verify the work with a test or a clear metric or whether it requires my judgment. Then propose one subjective task for me to focus on and a list of verifiable tasks that can run in the background.


DECIDE WHAT COMES BACK TO YOU

Constantly switching between agent threads to approve small decisions left senior editor Jack Cheng https://every.?ev_audience=free, another member of the frontier team, feeling scattered. He now lets agents act on their own when he can undo the result, like pushing code for a project that isn’t public. He still signs off on publishing a piece, buying something, or making a design choice without an obvious answer.

Jack also deputized Pip, his personal agent, as a chief of staff. Pip talks to project coordinators, blocks time, and triages tasks from Notion and Slack. It gives him a single-screen HTML brief with what he needs to know and what he needs to decide.

Jannik Jung, an engineer on the frontier team, usually has several experiments running at once across Claude Code and Codex. One of his major projects is our AI copy editor, KateBench https://every.?ev_audience=free, and experiments with it can take hours to return results. Working this way, he says, makes him “10 times as productive”: He focuses on a task for 10 or 15 minutes and then lets it run for hours. He’s “always been quite good at context switching,” he says, but sometimes a thread finishes unnoticed and sits waiting for him. When he does return to it, he needs to get back up to speed before he can do “the actual thinking again” about what needs to happen next. So when he refocuses on a project, he gives himself 15 to 30 minutes to ask the agent what happened, where things stand, and what needs his input before making any decisions.

He’s also changing what outputs agents bring back to him. He’s building his own orchestrator, a separate harness, to “lift the work one level up,” from managing agent sessions to working on goals and plans. The existing tools he tried left him either managing sessions or without an overview of what needed his input. His version is in early alpha, but he’s already using it on multiple projects. Jannik gives its main thread a mandate for what it can and can’t do, and it turns their discussions into a plan of tasks and dependencies. Each day, it gives him a brief on what happened and what he needs to decide, which he can act on without opening every session.

He describes his job as setting direction and checking whether results work for the intended user, not just whether they pass automated tests. Like Jack, he often lets agents merge and deploy code, but consequential or externally facing decisions come back to him. Jannik is still exploring how much freedom and what permissions he can give the orchestrator while still feeling in control, aware of what’s going on, and able to shape where something is going.

Try it: The next time you return to a project with several agent threads, ask for decisions instead of just a recap. Have the agent end its summary with the choices only you can make.

Prompt

I’m giving [project] my full attention for the next [15–30] minutes. Look across our subthreads for the latest updates and give me a short brief in three parts: what happened since [last check-in], where things stand, and the decisions that need me. For each decision, give the options and your recommendation. Treat anything consequential or externally facing, like [deploying, messaging a customer, publishing], as a decision for me. Put the brief on a single-screen HTML page, leading with the calls I need to make. Don’t take any action, change any permissions, or start new work. Flag any thread whose status you can’t tell. Then wait for my decisions.


WHEN THE SWITCHING WORKS

As the general manager of the Every Agent team, Marcus Moretti https://every.?ev_audience=free typically has three to five agent threads running in parallel, each covering a discrete area of work: Every Agent (EA) Billing, EA Funnel, and EA Frontier Alerts. Each thread acts like an engineering or product manager, working with Marcus to spin up subagents that do the work.

Marcus rotates between threads, dropping in during a pause in the work to unblock decisions, review proposals, or merge code. To prioritize among the things that need his input, he uses a simple framework: “Things that are urgent come first. Second is whether the thread has more work that is blocked—I want to unblock those so I can proceed to the next thread. Third is what I find interesting, for example, an analysis I’m looking forward to seeing.”

While Marcus is context-switching many times throughout the day, he feels empowered rather than drained because it means much more work is happening across different areas of the business. “It’s just how I operate now… If I didn’t use a multi-agent workspace, I’d barely get anything done.” He credits years of managing teams, where switching contexts all day was normal. It took some getting used to, but eventually it became routine. Managing agent threads, he says, is like going from one unrelated meeting to another or between Slack threads on different projects.

Mike Taylor https://every.?ev_audience=free, Every’s head of evals and a member of the frontier team, keeps his setup simple. He usually has five or six agent threads running, with one GitHub folder per project and one thread per piece of work. One agent reads the Notion backlog for the personal benchmarks https://every.?ev_audience=free product he works on and tells him what to tackle next. He opens a new thread for each item and merges the results as pull requests. He tried more elaborate orchestration frameworks, or “software factories,” but found he was spending too much time organizing the work.

Mike says that most of his time goes into redoing work or steering a thread until it gets things right. In one video-analysis experiment, he realized the agent was making up context without looking at the PowerPoint images. He had to tell it to go back and look.

“I feel very unfocused and scattered across lots of different projects, and it’s super-painful and exhausting to do,” Mike says. “But it’s also really fun, and I’m getting a lot done.” Coming back to a thread that did well is fun. Finding that one he didn’t prompt correctly has wasted six hours is frustrating. His rule is simple: “I don’t mind living in a mess for a while if I’m getting good work done.”

Try it: Even a week that feels disorganized can be productive. Before you clean up your threads at the end of the week, ask an agent what each one accomplished. You may have done more than it felt like at the time.

Prompt

Look across my agent sessions, [repos or pull requests], and [task tracker, e.g., Notion or Linear] from [this week]. For each line of work, tell me in a sentence what it actually produced: merged or shipped, still in progress, redone after a wrong start, or stalled. Note where I had to steer it back on track, and flag any thread that ran a long time without producing anything useful. Then tell me which threads look worth the scatter and which are costing more attention than they return. Don’t propose a new system for organizing them; I only want to know what the mess produced. This is a read-only review. Don’t reorganize, rename, close, or merge anything, and don’t post or message anyone. Anything about what to publish or share is my call. If you can’t see my sessions, tell me what you can’t reach and ask for the smallest thing that would help, like a list of thread names.


KEEP SIGHT OF THE ‘WHY’

Designer Mike Deal’s first major project at Every was Dan Shipper https://every.?ev_audience=free’s piece on Codex https://every.?ev_audience=free, which meant developing the article’s custom UX and several animated illustrations at once. Mike used a single “dispatcher” agent to coordinate the work and delegate tasks to other sessions. “I was able to move much faster than I ever have for editorial design,” he says.

The dispatcher’s speed came with coordination problems. Similar tasks sometimes went to different sessions, producing inconsistent results, and Mike couldn’t reliably tell which tasks were blocked or complete. A recurring status check consumed too many tokens, and his experiments with an HTML status board weren’t working well enough yet.

Using models that are fast but produce high-quality work helps. Grok 4.5 was the first that answered quickly enough to keep Mike on one task and in a flow state. Even so, the dispatcher passes along every subagent question it thinks needs his input, and enough of those can pull him into the weeds.

That’s when he needs to step back. “It’s too easy to lose sight of the ultimate goal because I’ve been rabbit-holing down into some sub-goal of a sub-goal,” Mike says. What helps is taking a pause, “ideally accompanied by a record-scratch sound,” to ask, “What are we actually trying to do and why?”

Try it: When you’re feeling overwhelmed or can’t find your focus, stop and step back. Have your orchestrator rebuild the picture from the top-level goal before it hands out any more work.

Prompt

Pause before you hand out any new work and leave running sessions alone.
1. Name the top-level goal of this whole project, not the current task: what the finished thing is, who it’s for, and why it matters. Say which parts I told you and which you’re inferring.
2. Trace the chain from that goal down to what I’ve been working on in the last few turns, one line per level.
3. Set the current task list aside. If we started today with only the top-level goal, what three things would matter most?
4. Now compare. Sort everything in flight or waiting on me into needed for the goal, nice to have, or drifted. Work already done is no reason to keep going.
5. Tell me what you’d stop, what you’d park, and the one thing I should do next.


WHAT I’M TRYING NEXT

After chatting with nine of my colleagues, I realized I wasn’t a unique flower. Delegating to many agents is exhilarating, and it is also exhausting. Everyone has a different approach, but a few habits came up again and again. My colleagues all pull decisions and strategic judgment into one place (like an orchestrator thread), give agents room to act on their own within guardrails, and step back to see the bigger picture when they lose the thread.

If working with AI has taught me anything, it’s that AI is an excellent teacher https://every.?ev_audience=free. So I did what I always do, and I asked Codex, “Can you read this article and based on how you know I work, pick an experiment for me to try to keep myself from getting so distracted? Which technique or framework would jibe best with how I use you currently?”

It recommended Lee’s approach, with one task that needs my judgment in the foreground and verifiable work running in the background, and gave me a great prompt to boot:

Prompt

For the next 45 minutes, I’m focusing on [one decision or draft]. I’ll call it done when [concrete outcome]. Pick one bounded task you can do in the background with a clear way to check the result. If you hit a decision that needs me, set that part aside and keep going where you can. If I bring up something unrelated in this chat, capture it in one line for after the block. When I check back, give me the result and any decisions that still need me.

Then Codex introduced accountability: After every block, it suggested I jot down whether I reached the outcome I wanted and how many times I switched to unrelated work. This would help me determine whether I could reach a decision or finish a draft while it worked on other projects in the background.

I’ll give it a try and report back. Sebastian can already tell me when I’ve worked on seven things in 29 minutes. I’d like our next conversation to be about which of those things needed me.
